title: Feelings aren't deeds (Tanya 12)
hookLine: the "in-between" person feels the pull but never acts on it
tomorrow: how far away is the good you're reaching for, really?

lines: THE TANYA GIVES IT A NAME.
cards: Someone cuts in front of you in line, and a sharp sentence rises all the way to your teeth. You don't say it. You let it go by.

Nobody will ever know it was there. So, yesterday's question: if you feel the pull and never act on it, does that count for anything? The Tanya says it counts for a great deal, and gives that person a name.

teach.b: The Tanya, by Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, calls that person the beinoni, the in-between. Not the tzaddik, the righteous one whose bad pull has gone quiet. Not the wicked one.
The beinoni still feels the pull: anger, envy, the cruel line, rising from the heart. But in chapter twelve, the Tanya says the beinoni never lets it into deliberate thought, or speech, or action.
The mind rules the heart, each time it rises.

teach.h: THE PULL RISES. THE HANDS STAY STILL.
teach.b: Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: by the Tanya's own definition, the beinoni has never acted on a bad pull and still isn't called righteous, because the pull is still there.
And the Tanya says this level is one every person can reach. Feelings come. They aren't deeds.

Muslims hand down a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the collection of al-Bukhari: God has pardoned his community for what their minds whisper to them, so long as they don't act on it or speak it.
What's shared is the line itself: a feeling that rises is not the same as a deed done.
And an honest difference. The hadith speaks of God's pardon for what crosses the mind.
The Tanya draws a whole way of living for the in-between person, who meets the pull again and again, and each time lets the mind decide.

how: In Chabad and other Hasidic communities the Tanya is studied daily in a set portion, and the beinoni is taught as a goal within reach rather than an excuse.

o: one who feels the pull and never acts on it
a student between beginner and scholar
an average person, half good and half bad

games.q: three kinds of people in the Tanya — tap the pairs.
p: feels the pull, never acts on it
the bad pull has gone quiet
the whisper unacted on is pardoned

s: a beinoni is a so-so person who sometimes slips
in the Tanya, the beinoni never acts on the pull in speech or deed.
in the Tanya, the beinoni still feels the pull
that's why the beinoni isn't called righteous: the pull is still there.
the hadith says a passing thought is held against a person
it says God has pardoned what minds whisper, so long as it isn't acted on or spoken.

games.q: your little brother says he must be a bad person because he wanted to hit his friend, even though he didn't. what does the Tanya give you to say?
o: wanting isn't doing: you felt it and didn't act, and that's the work.
you're fine, because good people never feel things like that.
you're right to worry; the feeling itself is the wrong you did.
games.why: the beinoni feels the pull and the mind rules the heart. feelings come; they aren't deeds.

practice: Sit still, and close your eyes if that's comfortable. Bring up one feeling that has been pulling at you lately: irritation, envy, a craving.
Don't shove it away and don't follow it; let it be there, and notice that your hands stay still. Rest in that gap between the pull and the deed for the length of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Beinoni: the Tanya's in-between person, who feels the pull and never lets it reach speech or action.

orig.note: Hebrew: in-between, the Tanya's name for one who feels the pull and never acts on it.

carryVoice: Feelings aren't deeds: the pull can come, and the hands can stay still. That's day two of the new block.

sources.ref: Tanya, Likutei Amarim ch. 12 (the beinoni: evil never reaches thought, speech or deed; the mind rules the heart)
Tanya, Likutei Amarim ch. 14 (the level of beinoni is attainable by every person)
